topics.h: A lump of clay is just mud, until a potter in Khurja turns it into a cup. When does something become a resource?
p: A resource is anything that people can use to meet a need, provided they have the knowledge and technology to use it and it is useful and valued.
Natural resources come from nature, for example air, water, soil, sunlight, forests, minerals and wildlife.
Human-made resources are things people make by changing natural resources, such as roads, bridges, buildings, machines and dams.
People themselves, with their skills, knowledge and health, are a resource too. They are called human resources.
Something can become a resource over time. Petroleum was of little use until people learnt how to refine it and build engines that run on it.

ex.q: Think it through: Is the wind blowing over the coast of Tamil Nadu a resource?
st: Ask: can people use it to meet a need?
Wind can turn the blades of wind turbines and make electricity.
India has the technology to build such turbines, and many stand along that coast.
So people value it and can use it.
ex.a: Yes. Wind is a natural resource because we have the technology to turn it into electricity.

topics.rl: Every time you drink water, switch on a fan or ride a bus over a bridge, you are using natural or human-made resources.

topics.h: Sunlight will shine on your terrace tomorrow, but the coal burnt in a power plant today is gone forever. Why the difference?
p: Renewable resources are renewed by nature quickly, within a human lifetime, for example sunlight, wind, water and forests.
Some renewable resources can still run short if we overuse them. Cutting forests faster than they regrow or polluting rivers harms them.
Non-renewable resources take millions of years to form, so once used they cannot be replaced in our lifetime. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are examples.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are called fossil fuels because they formed from the remains of plants and animals buried long ago.
Resources are spread unevenly. Some regions have plenty of a mineral or of water while others have very little, so regions depend on each other and trade.

ex.q: Think it through: A village switches from diesel pumps to solar pumps for watering fields. Which resource is it saving, and why does that matter?
st: Diesel is made from petroleum, a fossil fuel.
Petroleum takes millions of years to form, so it is non-renewable.
Sunlight is renewed every day, so it is renewable.
Using sunlight saves petroleum for the future and also causes less air pollution.
ex.a: It saves petroleum, a non-renewable resource, by using sunlight, a renewable one.

topics.rl: The solar panels on rooftops and the wind turbines in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu use renewable resources, while most cars still run on petrol or diesel from petroleum.

topics.h: If you eat all the mangoes on a tree and also chop the tree down, what will you eat next summer?
p: Sustainable use means using resources to meet our needs today without harming the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
Overuse and waste harm resources: cutting forests, over-pumping groundwater, overfishing and polluting rivers are examples.
We can conserve resources with the 3 Rs: Reduce what we use, Reuse things, and Recycle materials.
Many Indian communities have long protected nature, for example sacred groves, rainwater harvesting in stepwells and tanks, and the Bishnoi tradition of protecting trees and animals.
Mahatma Gandhi's idea is often quoted: the Earth provides enough to satisfy every person's need, but not every person's greed.

ex.q: Think it through: A school in Chennai collects rainwater from its roof into an underground tank. How is this sustainable?
st: Rain that falls on the roof would otherwise run off into drains.
The tank stores it, or lets it soak into the ground to refill groundwater.
The school pumps less groundwater for gardening and cleaning.
Groundwater is saved for the future.
ex.a: Rainwater harvesting saves and refills groundwater, so the resource lasts for the future.

topics.rl: Switching off fans when you leave a room, carrying a cloth bag to the market and giving old books to younger students are all ways to use resources sustainably.

topics.h: For more than 300 years, five different ruling families took turns on one throne in Delhi. Who were they?
p: The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206 CE, when Qutb-ud-din Aibak became Sultan in Delhi. It lasted until 1526 CE.
Five dynasties ruled one after another: the Mamluks (also called the Slave dynasty), the Khaljis, the Tughlaqs, the Sayyids and the Lodis.
Razia Sultan ruled from 1236 to 1240 CE. She was the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate.

Alauddin Khalji fixed the prices of goods in Delhi's markets and kept a large army that pushed back several Mongol attacks. Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri) and introduced token coins of copper and brass.
In 1398 CE, Timur from Central Asia attacked and plundered Delhi, which weakened the Sultanate. The last Sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, was defeated by Babur in 1526 CE.

ex.q: Think it through: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token coins failed. Why might token money fail if it is easy to copy?
st: A token coin is worth more than the metal it is made of; its value depends on the ruler's order.
Copper and brass were easy to get, so many people made fake coins at home.
The market was flooded with coins and people lost trust in them.
The Sultan had to withdraw the coins and exchange them for real gold and silver ones.
ex.a: Because the coins could be forged easily, too many fake coins spread, trust collapsed and the scheme had to be withdrawn.

topics.rl: You can still visit the Qutub Minar in Delhi, begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak and completed by Iltutmish, and the ruins of Tughlaqabad fort.

topics.h: In 1526 a ruler from Central Asia won a battle at Panipat with the help of cannons and guns. His family would rule for over 300 years.
p: Babur, a ruler from Fergana in Central Asia, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 and founded the Mughal empire. He used cannons and guns along with skilled cavalry.

His son Humayun lost his kingdom to Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and won it back in 1555. Sher Shah improved roads such as the one now called the Grand Trunk Road and issued a silver coin called the rupiya.
Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605. He organised officials through the mansabdari system, in which each officer held a rank, and followed a policy of sulh-i-kul, peace among all.
Later emperors were Jahangir, Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, and Aurangzeb, who ruled from 1658 to 1707. Under Aurangzeb the empire reached its largest size.
After Aurangzeb died in 1707, the empire grew weak and many regional powers, such as the Marathas, rose.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the mansabdari system help Akbar control a huge empire?
st: Every mansabdar (officer) was given a rank (mansab).
The rank decided his pay and the number of soldiers and horses he had to keep.
Mansabdars could be transferred and promoted or demoted by the emperor.
So all officers depended on the emperor, and he always had an army ready.
ex.a: It ranked every officer, tied their pay to soldiers they maintained and kept them loyal to the emperor, giving him a ready army and an organised government.

topics.rl: The word 'rupee' on our banknotes comes from the rupiya, the silver coin issued by Sher Shah Suri.

topics.h: While Delhi saw Sultans and Mughals, powerful kingdoms ruled the Deccan, Rajasthan, Gondwana and Assam, and many of them fought hard to stay free.
p: The Vijayanagara empire was founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka. Its capital, Vijayanagara (Hampi), lay on the Tungabhadra river and was a rich trading city.
Krishnadevaraya was Vijayanagara's most famous ruler. In 1565, at the Battle of Talikota, an alliance of Deccan Sultanates defeated Vijayanagara and the capital was ruined.
Rajput rulers of Mewar resisted the Mughals. Rana Sanga fought Babur at Khanwa in 1527, and Maharana Pratap fought Akbar's army at Haldighati in 1576.
Rani Durgavati of Garha-Katanga (in Gondwana, central India) fought Mughal forces bravely in 1564.
The Ahoms of Assam resisted the Mughals. In 1671, their commander Lachit Borphukan won the Battle of Saraighat on the Brahmaputra river.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the Brahmaputra help the Ahoms at Saraighat?
st: The battle was fought on the river near Guwahati.
The Ahoms knew the river, its currents and its narrow points well.
They used boats skilfully and built defences along the banks.
So the Mughal fleet could not use its larger numbers well.
ex.a: The Ahoms used their knowledge of the river and good boat warfare, so the geography worked in their favour.

topics.rl: You can walk among the ruins of Hampi in Karnataka, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The National Defence Academy awards a Lachit Borphukan gold medal to its best cadet.

topics.h: A boy who grew up among the hills of the Sahyadris went on to build a kingdom from a handful of forts. His name was Shivaji.
p: Shivaji was born in 1630 at Shivneri fort near Pune. His father was Shahaji Bhonsle and his mother was Jijabai, who shaped his values and courage.
He began by capturing hill forts in the Sahyadris (Western Ghats) and built up swarajya, his own self-rule.
In 1659 he defeated Afzal Khan, a general of the Bijapur Sultanate, at Pratapgad. In 1666 he made a famous escape from Aurangzeb's custody in Agra.
His soldiers used guerrilla warfare: small, fast groups that knew the hills well and struck by surprise.
In 1674 he was crowned at Raigad fort and took the title Chhatrapati. He died in 1680.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did guerrilla warfare suit the Marathas in the Sahyadri hills?
st: The Sahyadris have steep slopes, narrow passes and thick forests.
Large armies with heavy guns and elephants move slowly there.
Small Maratha bands knew every path and could attack quickly and vanish.
Hill forts gave them safe bases to rest and store supplies.
ex.a: The rough hills slowed big armies, while small, fast Maratha groups who knew the land could strike and retreat to their forts.

topics.rl: Shivneri, Raigad and Pratapgad still stand in Maharashtra, and many school trips climb these forts every year.

topics.h: A king cannot run a kingdom alone. Shivaji had a team of eight ministers, a navy and a ring of strong forts.
p: Shivaji was helped by a council of eight ministers called the Ashtapradhan. The Peshwa was the chief minister.
Forts were the backbone of his kingdom. He built and repaired many, including sea forts like Sindhudurg on the Konkan coast.
He built a navy to protect the coast and trade from foreign powers such as the Portuguese and the Siddis of Janjira.
He collected chauth, one-fourth (25%) of the revenue, and sardeshmukhi, an extra one-tenth (10%), from areas outside his direct rule.
He paid many soldiers and officials in cash instead of giving them land, so that they stayed loyal to the state.

ex.q: Think it through: A district's land revenue is ₹1,000. If the Marathas collected chauth from it, how much would that be?
st: Chauth means one-fourth of the revenue.
One-fourth of ₹1,000 = 1000 ÷ 4.

topics.rl: Sindhudurg sea fort near Malvan was built on an island; boats still carry visitors there. The Indian Navy honours Shivaji's naval vision.

topics.h: From the hills of Maharashtra, Maratha horsemen rode as far as Delhi, Odisha and the Punjab within a hundred years of Shivaji.
p: After Shivaji, his sons Sambhaji and Rajaram, and later Rajaram's widow Tarabai, kept fighting the Mughals in the Deccan.
In the 18th century, the Peshwas became the real leaders of the Maratha state, with Pune as their centre. Bajirao I led campaigns deep into north India.
Maratha chiefs set up their own strong states: the Holkars at Indore, the Scindias (Shindes) at Gwalior, the Gaekwads at Baroda and the Bhonsles at Nagpur.
In 1761 the Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat to Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan, but they soon recovered much of their power.

Ahilyabai Holkar, who ruled from Maheshwar, is remembered for good administration and for building and repairing temples, ghats and wells across India. The Marathas were finally defeated by the British in 1818.

ex.q: Think it through: Why is the Maratha state of the 18th century often called a confederacy?
st: A confederacy is a group of states joined together.
The Peshwa at Pune was the overall leader.
Chiefs like the Holkars, Scindias, Gaekwads and Bhonsles ruled their own regions.
They worked together, though they were quite independent in their own areas.
ex.a: Because several powerful Maratha chiefs ruled their own states while accepting the Peshwa as their head.

topics.rl: The royal palaces of Gwalior and Baroda and the ghats of Maheshwar on the Narmada are reminders of the Maratha chiefs.

topics.t: Traders from Europe and the East India Company
topics.h: European ships sailed for months around Africa to reach India. They came for pepper, cloves and fine cotton cloth, not to rule. So how did one company end up governing India?
p: In 1498, the Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode) on the Malabar coast by sailing around Africa. This opened a sea route from Europe to India.
The Portuguese, the Dutch, the English and the French all set up trading companies to buy Indian spices, cotton and silk cloth, and indigo.
The English East India Company was given a royal charter by Queen Elizabeth I in 1600, which gave it the sole right among English merchants to trade with the East.
The Company built trading posts called factories, often protected by forts. Its main centres became Madras (Fort St George), Bombay and Calcutta (Fort William).
The European companies competed fiercely, and the English and French fought each other in south India in the 18th century.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did a trading company need forts and soldiers?
st: The companies were rivals and often attacked each other's ships and posts.
They wanted to protect their warehouses full of goods.
Soldiers and forts also let them put pressure on local rulers.
Over time, this military power turned the Company from a trader into a ruler.
ex.a: To protect goods from rivals, and because armed power let the Company press local rulers; this later helped it take over territory.

topics.rl: Fort St George in Chennai still stands and houses the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. Kozhikode's Kappad beach has a memorial marking Vasco da Gama's landing.

topics.h: In 1757, a battle in a mango grove at Plassey in Bengal changed the course of Indian history. How did a trading company win a kingdom?
p: At the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive of the Company defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal. Mir Jafar, the Nawab's commander, had secretly sided with the Company.

At the Battle of Buxar in 1764, the Company defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. In 1765 it received the Diwani of Bengal, the right to collect revenue.
The Company fought wars with Mysore, ruled by Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan. Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799. It also fought and finally defeated the Marathas by 1818.
Policies such as the Subsidiary Alliance and Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse were used to bring more kingdoms under Company control.
Anger built up and in 1857 a great revolt broke out, beginning with sepoys at Meerut on 10 May. After it, the British Crown took over rule from the Company in 1858.

ex.q: Think it through: Under the Doctrine of Lapse, a ruler died without a son born to him. What happened to his kingdom, and why did this anger people?
st: Indian rulers often adopted a son as heir when they had no son of their own.
The Doctrine of Lapse refused to accept an adopted son as heir.
So the kingdom 'lapsed', meaning it was taken over by the Company.
Kingdoms like Satara and Jhansi were taken this way, and rulers and people resented it.
ex.a: The kingdom was taken over by the Company, which angered rulers like Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi.

topics.rl: Statues, roads and schools across India are named after Rani Lakshmibai and other leaders of the struggle against Company rule.

topics.h: Indian cotton cloth was once wanted all over the world. Yet by the 19th century, many Indian weavers had lost their work. What happened?
p: The British changed land revenue systems. Under the Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal, introduced by Lord Cornwallis, zamindars had to pay a fixed revenue, and peasants were often squeezed hard.
Cheap machine-made cloth from British factories flooded Indian markets, while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain. Many weavers and artisans lost their livelihoods.
Farmers were pushed to grow crops like indigo and cotton for export instead of food. Famines, such as the Bengal famine of 1770, caused terrible suffering.
Dadabhai Naoroji explained the 'drain of wealth': India's wealth flowed to Britain through salaries, profits and payments.

Railways (the first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853), telegraph and English education spread, mainly to serve British needs. Indian reformers, newspapers and the new educated class later used these to spread ideas of freedom.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the first railway lines mostly link ports with places where raw materials were produced?
st: Britain wanted raw cotton, indigo and other goods for its factories.
Trains carried these cheaply from the interior to ports like Bombay and Calcutta.
Ships took them to Britain, and British goods came back to be sold in India.
So railways mainly served colonial trade, though Indians also began to travel and share ideas.
ex.a: They were built mainly to move raw materials to ports and British goods into India, serving colonial trade.

topics.rl: The handloom weavers of Varanasi, Chanderi and Kanchipuram keep India's great textile tradition alive, and National Handloom Day is celebrated on 7 August.

topics.ch: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System
topics.t: Universal adult franchise: the right to vote
topics.h: A farmer in a Ladakh village and a business owner in Mumbai each get exactly one vote, and both votes count equally. That is a powerful idea!
p: Franchise means the right to vote. Universal adult franchise means every adult citizen can vote, whatever their religion, caste, gender, wealth, education or region.
India's Constitution gave universal adult franchise from the very beginning in 1950. The first general elections were held in 1951–52.
The voting age was at first 21 years. The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act of 1988 lowered it to 18 years.
Many countries gave women the vote only after long struggles; Switzerland allowed women to vote in national elections only in 1971. India gave women and men the vote together from the start.
The principle is 'one person, one vote, one value': every vote has the same weight.

ex.q: Think it through: Why was it a bold decision to give every adult the vote in 1951–52, when many people could not read?
st: Many people said only educated or property-owning people should vote.
India's leaders believed every citizen, rich or poor, had the right to choose the government.
Party symbols were printed so that people who could not read could still recognise their choice.
This trusted ordinary people and made democracy belong to everyone.
ex.a: It trusted every adult, educated or not, with an equal say, and symbols made voting possible for all.

topics.rl: When an older sibling turns 18, they can enrol as a voter and get a voter ID card (EPIC) from the Election Commission.

topics.ch: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System
topics.h: India holds the biggest elections in the world, with crores of voters and lakhs of polling booths. Who makes sure they are free and fair?
p: The Election Commission of India (ECI) was set up on 25 January 1950 under Article 324 of the Constitution. 25 January is celebrated as National Voters' Day.
It is an independent constitutional body, so no government can order it to favour any party.
It is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner, along with other Election Commissioners. Sukumar Sen was India's first Chief Election Commissioner.

It conducts elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and Councils, and the offices of President and Vice-President. State Election Commissions conduct panchayat and municipal elections.
It prepares voter lists (electoral rolls), issues voter ID cards and enforces the Model Code of Conduct, rules that parties and candidates must follow during elections.

ex.q: Think it through: Why is it important that the Election Commission is independent of the government?
st: The party in power also contests the election.
If the government controlled the referee, it could bend the rules for itself.
An independent Commission applies the same rules to every party.
This keeps voters' trust in the result.
ex.a: Because the ruling party is also a player; an independent referee applies rules equally and keeps elections fair.

topics.rl: Before elections, you may see posters saying 'No voter to be left behind' and booth officers going door to door to check voter lists.

topics.ch: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System
topics.h: On voting day, you press a button, a beep sounds and a tiny slip flashes behind glass. What happens before and after that moment?
p: The country is divided into constituencies. Each constituency elects one representative. There are 543 Lok Sabha constituencies.
Candidates file nominations, and parties and candidates campaign. A citizen must be at least 25 years old to contest a Lok Sabha or Assembly election.
Voting is by secret ballot using Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs). A VVPAT machine shows a paper slip so the voter can check the vote. Indelible ink is put on the voter's left index finger.
The candidate who gets the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority of all votes. This is called the first-past-the-post system.

Some constituencies are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes so they are fairly represented. Voters who do not wish to choose any candidate can press NOTA (None of the Above), available since 2013.

ex.q: Think it through: In a constituency, A gets 45,000 votes, B gets 35,000 and C gets 20,000. Who wins, and did the winner get more than half the votes?
st: A has the most votes, so A wins (first-past-the-post).
Half of 1,00,000 is 50,000; A's 45,000 is less than half.
So A wins without a majority of all votes.
ex.a: A wins with 45,000 votes, though that is less than half of the 1,00,000 votes cast.

topics.rl: After voting, people proudly show their inked finger. The ink stays for days, so no one can vote twice.

topics.ch: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
topics.t: Parliament: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
topics.h: India's laws are made in a Parliament with two Houses. Why two? Isn't one enough?
p: The Parliament of India has three parts: the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
Members of the Lok Sabha are elected directly by the people. 543 members are elected, one from each constituency, for a term of five years. The Lok Sabha can be dissolved earlier.
The Speaker, elected by Lok Sabha members, presides over the Lok Sabha.

The Rajya Sabha represents the states and union territories. Most of its members are elected by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, and the President nominates 12 members known for art, literature, science or social service. It can have at most 250 members.
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved. Each member serves six years, and one-third of the members retire every two years. The Vice-President of India is its Chairman.

ex.q: Think it through: The Lok Sabha is dissolved, but bills still need careful review. Why is it useful to have a second House that is never dissolved?
st: The Rajya Sabha continues even when the Lok Sabha is dissolved.
Its members change in batches every two years, so experienced members are always present.
It gives a second look at bills passed by the Lok Sabha.
It also lets the states have a voice in making national laws.
ex.a: A permanent second House gives continuity, experienced review of laws and a voice for the states.

topics.rl: On TV channels like Sansad TV, you can watch members debating in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

topics.ch: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
topics.h: Every law begins as an idea written on paper called a bill. It must survive debates in two Houses before it becomes law.
p: A proposed law is called a bill. It can be introduced by a minister or by any member of Parliament.
A bill is debated, discussed in committees and voted on. It must be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
After both Houses pass it, the bill goes to the President. Once the President gives assent, it becomes an Act, a law.
A Money Bill, about taxes and government spending, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can only suggest changes and must return it within 14 days.
Parliament also keeps a check on the government. During Question Hour, members ask ministers questions, and they debate the government's work and budget.

ex.q: Think it through: Why must a bill pass both Houses and also get the President's assent?
st: Two Houses mean two rounds of debate, so mistakes can be caught.
The Lok Sabha speaks for the people directly, the Rajya Sabha for the states.
The President's assent is the final formal step.
These checks make sure laws are made carefully, not in a hurry.
ex.a: Several stages of debate and approval make law-making careful and include the views of people and states.

topics.rl: Laws you have heard of, such as the Right to Education Act, began as bills in Parliament.

topics.ch: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
topics.t: The executive: President, Prime Minister and Cabinet
topics.h: The President is India's head, yet the Prime Minister runs the government. How do both fit together?
p: The executive carries out laws and runs the government. India follows the parliamentary system, in which the executive comes from the legislature and answers to it.

The President is the head of the State. The President is elected by an electoral college of elected members of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies, and generally acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
The Prime Minister is the head of the government. The President appoints as Prime Minister the leader who has the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha.
The Prime Minister chooses ministers, who are appointed by the President. The senior ministers form the Cabinet. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the Council of Ministers must resign. Civil servants, such as IAS officers, form the permanent executive that carries out decisions.

ex.q: Think it through: What does 'collective responsibility' mean for the Council of Ministers?
st: All ministers stand together for the government's decisions.
They are answerable as one team to the Lok Sabha.
If the Lok Sabha loses confidence in the government, the whole Council of Ministers must resign, not just one minister.
So the government must keep the support of the people's representatives.
ex.a: The ministers act as one team, answer together to the Lok Sabha, and resign together if it loses confidence in them.

topics.rl: When the news says 'The Cabinet approved a new scheme', it means the senior ministers led by the Prime Minister took a decision together.

topics.h: To make one cup of masala chai, you need tea leaves from Assam, milk from a dairy, sugar from sugarcane fields and someone to brew it. All goods need the same basic ingredients, called factors of production.
p: Production means making goods or providing services. The things needed for production are called factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
In economics, land means all natural resources used in production, such as soil, water, minerals, forests and the land surface itself.
Land is limited in quantity; we cannot create more of it. The payment for the use of land is called rent.
Labour is the physical and mental effort of people in production, for example a farmer ploughing, a teacher teaching or an engineer designing. The payment for labour is called wages.
When people gain education, training and good health, their labour becomes more productive. This is called human capital.

ex.q: Think it through: A potter in Kutch makes clay pots. Identify the land and labour in his work.
st: The clay comes from the earth and water comes from a well or river: these are land.
The potter shaping the pot on his wheel is giving labour.
His skill, learnt over years, is human capital that makes his labour better.
Without both land and labour, there would be no pot.
ex.a: Clay and water are land; the potter's effort and skill are labour (and his skill is human capital).

topics.rl: When your school hires a new teacher, it pays wages for labour; when a shopkeeper rents a shop, he pays rent for the use of land.

topics.h: A tailor with a needle stitches one shirt a day; with a sewing machine she stitches many. That machine is capital.
p: Capital means human-made goods used to produce other goods and services, along with the money used to buy them.
Fixed capital includes tools, machines and buildings that are used again and again over many years, such as a tractor, a loom or a factory shed.
Working capital includes raw materials and money in hand that get used up in production, such as cotton yarn for a weaver or flour for a baker.
Capital is made by people, unlike land. It wears out with use, so it must be repaired or replaced.
The payment for the use of money capital is called interest.

ex.q: Think it through: A baker in Bengaluru has an oven, flour, sugar and ₹5,000 to pay for gas. Sort these into fixed and working capital.
st: The oven is used for years: fixed capital.
Flour and sugar are used up in each batch: working capital.
The ₹5,000 cash for gas is spent in production: working capital.
So the oven is fixed capital; the flour, sugar and cash are working capital.
ex.a: Fixed capital: the oven. Working capital: flour, sugar and cash in hand.

topics.rl: When a farmer takes a loan from a bank to buy a pump, he pays interest; the pump becomes his fixed capital.

topics.h: Land, labour and capital are like ingredients on a kitchen shelf. Someone has to decide what to cook, and take the risk that no one likes it. That someone is the entrepreneur.
p: An entrepreneur organises land, labour and capital to produce goods or services.
Entrepreneurs take risks. If the business does well they earn a profit; if it does badly they bear the loss.
Entrepreneurs bring new ideas, called innovation, such as a new product, a cheaper method or a new market.
The reward for entrepreneurship is profit, which is what is left after paying rent, wages, interest and other costs.
Entrepreneurs create jobs and help an economy grow. Many young Indians now start small businesses and startups.

ex.q: Think it through: Meena opens a dosa stall. She earns ₹20,000 in a month. She pays ₹4,000 rent, ₹8,000 wages to a helper, ₹1,000 interest on a loan and ₹5,000 for raw materials. What is her profit?
st: Profit = earnings − costs = 20,000 − 18,000.
Profit = ₹2,000.
This profit is her reward for organising the stall and taking the risk.

topics.rl: Small shops in your area, food delivery startups and self-help groups making pickles or papad are all run by entrepreneurs.

topics.h: If you could fly around the Earth, you would cross seven great landmasses and five vast oceans. Where does India fit in?
p: The large landmasses of the Earth are called continents. There are seven: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
Asia is the largest continent, and it has the most people. India is in South Asia. Australia is the smallest continent.
Africa is the only continent crossed by the Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
Antarctica, around the South Pole, is covered by a thick ice sheet and has no permanent residents, only scientists at research stations. India runs research stations there called Maitri and Bharati.
There are five oceans: the Pacific (the largest and deepest), the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and the Arctic (the smallest). The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country.

ex.q: Think it through: A ship sails from Mumbai to the east coast of Africa. Which ocean does it cross?
st: Mumbai is on India's west coast, on the Arabian Sea.
The Arabian Sea is part of the Indian Ocean.
East Africa's coast also faces the Indian Ocean.
So the ship stays in the Indian Ocean all the way.
ex.a: The Indian Ocean.

topics.rl: Indian ships carry goods across the Indian Ocean, and Indian scientists travel every year to Maitri and Bharati in Antarctica.

topics.t: Grasslands and natural regions of the world
topics.h: The same kind of grassy plain has different names on every continent: Prairies, Pampas, Steppes, Veld, Downs and Savanna!
p: Places with similar climate, plants and animals form natural regions, such as hot deserts, tropical rainforests, grasslands and polar regions.
Tropical grasslands with tall grass and scattered trees are called savannas. The African savanna is home to lions, zebras, giraffes and elephants.
Temperate grasslands have different local names: Prairies in North America, Pampas in South America, Steppes in Europe and Asia, Veld in South Africa and Downs in Australia.
Temperate grasslands are among the world's great farming regions, growing wheat, maize and other crops and supporting large-scale cattle and sheep rearing.
In cold polar lands near the Arctic, the tundra has only mosses, lichens and small shrubs because the ground stays frozen for most of the year.

ex.q: Think it through: Why are the Prairies and the Pampas good for growing wheat?
st: Both are wide, mostly flat plains.
Their grasses, over thousands of years, made the soil deep and fertile.
They get moderate rainfall, enough for grass and grain crops.
Flat land also makes it easy to use machines for farming.
ex.a: Flat land, fertile soil and moderate rainfall make them ideal for wheat.

topics.rl: Some of the wheat and pulses traded around the world come from the Prairies of Canada and the Downs of Australia.

topics.t: World landscapes: mountains, deserts, rivers and forests
topics.h: The world's highest mountain peak, its largest hot desert and its largest rainforest are all on different continents. Let us visit them!
p: The Himalayas, to India's north, are the highest mountain range in the world. Mount Everest, the highest peak on Earth, lies on the border of Nepal and China.
The Andes along the west of South America form the longest mountain range on land. Other great ranges are the Rockies in North America and the Alps in Europe.
The Sahara in northern Africa is the largest hot desert. The Atacama in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth, and the Gobi in Asia is a cold desert.
The Amazon River in South America carries more water than any other river, and the Amazon basin has the largest tropical rainforest. The Nile flows north through Africa into the Mediterranean Sea.
The Great Barrier Reef off north-eastern Australia is the world's largest coral reef system.

ex.q: Think it through: Why do very few people live in the middle of the Sahara?
st: The Sahara gets very little rain.
Days are extremely hot and there is little fresh water.
Without water, crops cannot be grown and animals cannot be kept easily.
So people live mainly near oases and rivers like the Nile.
ex.a: Because there is very little water, people cluster near oases and the Nile instead.

topics.rl: Mountaineers from India, such as Bachendri Pal, the first Indian woman to climb Everest, have scaled the world's highest peaks.

topics.h: In 1885, about seventy Indians met in Bombay to discuss their country's problems. Few could have guessed that their meeting would grow into a movement of crores.
p: The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 at Bombay. W. C. Bonnerjee presided over its first session, and A. O. Hume, a retired British official, helped set it up.

Early leaders such as Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale are called Moderates. They used petitions, speeches and newspapers to ask for reforms and wrote about the economic harm of British rule.
In 1905, Lord Curzon divided the province of Bengal. Many saw this as a move to divide people, and it sparked the Swadeshi movement: people boycotted British goods and used Indian-made goods instead.

Leaders who demanded stronger action, such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal), are often called Radicals. Tilak declared, 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.'
Because of the strong protests, the partition of Bengal was cancelled in 1911.

ex.q: Think it through: How did boycotting British cloth during the Swadeshi movement put pressure on the British?
st: British mills earned huge profits by selling cloth in India.
When Indians stopped buying it, those sales fell.
Indian weavers and mills got more customers instead.
Lost profits and mass protest showed the British that Indians were united.
ex.a: It cut British profits, helped Indian industry and showed united public opposition.

topics.rl: The word 'swadeshi', meaning 'of one's own country', is still used today when people choose locally made goods.

topics.h: A thin man with a walking stick and a handful of salt shook the mighty British Empire. How?
p: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915. He used satyagraha, the method of truth and non-violent resistance.
His first satyagrahas in India were for indigo farmers at Champaran in Bihar (1917), peasants of Kheda in Gujarat (1918) and mill workers of Ahmedabad (1918).

On 13 April 1919, British troops under General Dyer fired on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, killing many people. The nation was deeply shocked. In 1920 Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement, which he withdrew in 1922 after violence at Chauri Chaura.

At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Congress demanded Purna Swaraj, complete independence. On 12 March 1930, Gandhi began the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to break the salt law, starting the Civil Disobedience Movement.
On 8 August 1942, the Quit India Movement was launched in Bombay with Gandhi's call 'Do or Die'.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did Gandhi choose salt for his protest in 1930?
st: Every person, rich or poor, needs salt.
The British had a monopoly on making salt and taxed it.
Making salt from sea water was simple, so anyone could break the law peacefully.
The protest united people across India in a simple, non-violent act.
ex.a: Salt was needed by all, the tax hurt the poor most, and anyone could break the salt law peacefully, so it united the whole country.

topics.rl: Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad and the Dandi memorial in Gujarat are visited by lakhs of people. 2 October, Gandhi's birthday, is also the International Day of Non-Violence.

topics.h: The freedom struggle had many heroes: speakers, writers, soldiers, farmers, students and women from every corner of India.
p: Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were young revolutionaries who were hanged by the British on 23 March 1931. 23 March is observed as Shaheed Diwas in their memory. Chandrashekhar Azad was another fearless revolutionary.
Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) with the call 'Dilli Chalo'. He is also remembered for the words 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom!'
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel led the Bardoli satyagraha of farmers in 1928. After independence, he played the key role in uniting the princely states with India.

Women leaders included Sarojini Naidu, the first Indian woman to preside over the Congress, and Aruna Asaf Ali, who hoisted the flag in Bombay at the start of the Quit India Movement. Rani Gaidinliu led resistance in the north-east.

India became independent on 15 August 1947, though the country was partitioned and India and Pakistan were formed. Jawaharlal Nehru became the first Prime Minister, and Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the committee that drafted the Constitution.

ex.q: Think it through: Why do historians say the freedom struggle was a 'people's movement' and not the work of one leader?
st: Leaders followed different paths: peaceful satyagraha, revolutionary action and the INA.
Farmers, workers, students and women joined protests across the country.
People from every region and community took part.
Together, this pressure made it impossible for British rule to continue.
ex.a: Because many leaders and lakhs of ordinary people from every region took part in different ways, and their combined effort won freedom.

topics.rl: Every year on 15 August, the Prime Minister hoists the national flag at the Red Fort in Delhi, and 23 January, Netaji's birthday, is celebrated as Parakram Diwas.

topics.t: Temple architecture: Nagara, Dravida and Vesara
topics.h: Look at the top of a temple. A curving tower, a stepped pyramid, or something in between? The shape tells you which style it follows!
p: A Hindu temple usually has a garbhagriha (the inner sanctum where the main deity is placed), a mandapa (a hall for devotees) and a tower above the sanctum.
In the Nagara style of north India, the tower is a curved shikhara. Examples are the Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho, built by the Chandelas, and the Sun Temple at Konark in Odisha.

In the Dravida style of south India, the tower over the sanctum is a pyramid-like vimana, and big gateway towers called gopurams stand at the entrances. The Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur, built by the Chola king Rajaraja I and completed around 1010 CE, is a famous example.
The Vesara style mixes Nagara and Dravida features. It developed in the Deccan under the Chalukyas and the Hoysalas.
Some temples were carved out of solid rock. The Kailasa temple at Ellora, built under the Rashtrakutas, was cut from a single rock from the top downwards.

ex.q: Think it through: You see a temple with a huge, decorated gateway tower at the entrance and a stepped, pyramid-shaped tower over the sanctum. Which style is it?
st: A big gateway tower is a gopuram.
A stepped, pyramid-shaped tower over the sanctum is a vimana.
Gopurams and vimanas are features of the Dravida style.
So it is most likely a south Indian Dravida temple.
ex.a: Dravida style.

topics.rl: The Konark Sun Temple appears on the back of the ₹10 note and the Ellora caves on the ₹20 note. Check the notes in your family's wallet!

topics.h: How do you hold up a huge roof without a forest of pillars? Builders in medieval India used arches and domes!
p: Older Indian buildings mostly used the trabeate (post-and-lintel) method: horizontal beams resting on upright pillars.
From the 13th century, the arcuate method of arches and domes became common. Combined with Indian decoration, this created Indo-Islamic architecture.
The Qutub Minar in Delhi, begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak and completed by Iltutmish, is a tall tower of red sandstone. The Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur has one of the largest domes in the world.

Mughal buildings include Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, set in a charbagh (a garden divided into four parts); the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri, built by Akbar; and the Taj Mahal in Agra and the Red Fort in Delhi, built by Shah Jahan.
India also has mighty forts built by many rulers, such as Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh in Rajasthan, Golconda near Hyderabad, Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh and Raigad in Maharashtra.

ex.q: Think it through: Why can an arch carry more weight across a wide opening than a flat stone beam?
st: A flat beam must bend to carry weight, and stone cracks easily when it bends.
An arch is made of wedge-shaped stones that press against each other.
The weight is pushed sideways and down into the pillars or walls.
So arches and domes can span wide spaces without many pillars.
ex.a: Because an arch passes the weight along its curve down into its supports, while a flat stone beam cracks if the gap is too wide.

topics.rl: The Red Fort appears on the ₹500 note, and the Prime Minister speaks from its ramparts every Independence Day.

topics.h: Some of India's oldest buildings were not built up from the ground but carved into hills, and some go down into the earth!
p: A stupa is a dome-shaped mound built over relics of the Buddha or Buddhist saints. The Great Stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh was first built in the time of Emperor Ashoka (3rd century BCE). Its stone gateways, called toranas, have carved stories.
Rock-cut caves were made for monks. A chaitya was a prayer hall and a vihara was a monastery. The Ajanta caves in Maharashtra are famous for their wall paintings.
Stepwells (vavs or baolis) were built to store water, with steps leading down to it. Rani ki Vav at Patan, Gujarat, built in the 11th century, is decorated with hundreds of carvings.
The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar is the holiest gurdwara of the Sikhs, with entrances on all four sides.
In the colonial period, the Indo-Saracenic style mixed Indian and European features, as in the Gateway of India in Mumbai and the Victoria Memorial in Kolkata.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did people in dry regions like Gujarat and Rajasthan build stepwells?
st: These regions get little rain, mostly in a few monsoon months.
Stepwells reached down to groundwater and stored rainwater.
Steps let people climb down to the water even when its level fell.
The shaded, cool steps were also a pleasant place to rest.
ex.a: To store and reach water through the dry months, since rain falls only for a short season.

topics.rl: Rani ki Vav is pictured on the ₹100 note and the Sanchi Stupa on the ₹200 note.

topics.ch: The Role of the Judiciary in Our Society
topics.h: Two neighbours in Nagpur quarrel over a wall. If they cannot settle it, where do they go, and what if one of them is unhappy with the decision?
p: The judiciary is the system of courts that interprets laws and settles disputes.
India has an integrated judiciary, like a pyramid. The Supreme Court is at the top, High Courts are in the states, and District Courts and other lower courts work at the district level.
If a person is not satisfied with a lower court's decision, they can usually appeal to a higher court.
The Supreme Court in New Delhi was set up on 28 January 1950. It is headed by the Chief Justice of India, who is appointed by the President. Its decisions must be followed by all courts in India.

The judiciary is independent: the government cannot tell judges how to decide, and judges cannot be easily removed. Courts can strike down laws that go against the Constitution; this is called judicial review.

ex.q: Think it through: A District Court decides a land dispute. One side thinks the decision is wrong. What can they do?
st: They can appeal to the High Court of their state.
The High Court checks whether the law was applied correctly.
If still unhappy, in some cases they can appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court's decision is final.
ex.a: Appeal to the High Court, and in some cases then to the Supreme Court, whose decision is final.

topics.rl: The Supreme Court's motto is 'Yato Dharmastato Jayah', meaning 'Where there is dharma (righteousness), there is victory.'

topics.ch: The Role of the Judiciary in Our Society
topics.h: Can a minister skip a red light because he is important? In a country with the rule of law, the answer is no.
p: The rule of law means that laws apply equally to everyone, and no one is above the law, whatever their position, wealth, religion or caste.
Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to all persons in India.
Laws must be made by the proper process, be known to the public, and be applied fairly. People can be punished only for breaking a law that exists.
Courts uphold the rule of law. Even the government must act according to law, and its actions can be challenged in court.
Without the rule of law, the powerful could do as they pleased, and ordinary people would have no protection.

ex.q: Think it through: A rich factory owner dumps waste into a river. Villagers complain. How does the rule of law help them?
st: Laws to protect the environment apply to everyone, rich or poor.
The villagers can approach the authorities or the court.
The court applies the same law to the owner as it would to anyone.
The owner can be ordered to stop and to pay for the damage.
ex.a: Because no one is above the law, the court can make even a powerful owner obey environmental laws.

topics.rl: When a traffic police officer fines a costly car for jumping a signal just as they would fine a scooter, that is the rule of law in action.

topics.ch: The Role of the Judiciary in Our Society
topics.h: A daily-wage worker cannot afford a lawyer. Does that mean she cannot get justice? Our system says no.
p: Criminal cases deal with acts that the law treats as crimes, such as theft or assault. A First Information Report (FIR) is usually filed with the police, and the guilty can be punished.
Civil cases deal with disputes about rights between people, such as over property, rent, contracts or divorce. The affected person files a case, and the court gives relief such as compensation.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) lets any person or group approach a High Court or the Supreme Court on behalf of people whose rights are violated. Courts have even accepted letters as PILs.
The Constitution (Article 39A) directs the State to provide free legal aid so that no one is denied justice because of poverty. Legal Services Authorities provide free lawyers to those who need them.
Lok Adalats (people's courts) settle disputes quickly by mutual agreement, with no court fee. Delays in courts are a challenge, as the saying 'justice delayed is justice denied' reminds us.

ex.q: Think it through: Ravi's tenant has not paid rent for six months. Is this a civil or a criminal case?
st: The dispute is about money owed under a rent agreement.
It is a disagreement over rights between two people.
Ravi himself would file the case asking for the rent.
Such disputes are civil cases.
ex.a: A civil case.

topics.rl: Many district courts hold Lok Adalats on weekends where cases such as traffic fines and bank loan disputes are settled in a single day.

topics.h: Your passport and voter ID say you are a citizen of India. But what does being a citizen really mean?
p: A citizen is a full member of a country, with rights given by its Constitution and laws, and duties towards the country.
Citizenship in India is governed by the Constitution and the Citizenship Act, 1955. It can be acquired by birth, by descent, by registration or by naturalisation.
India has single citizenship: a person is a citizen of India as a whole, not of a separate state.
Only citizens can vote, contest elections and hold certain high offices such as President, Vice-President and judge of the Supreme Court.
Citizenship is a two-way bond: the nation protects our rights, and we perform our duties to the nation and to fellow citizens.

ex.q: Think it through: Priya lives in Kerala and moves to Punjab for work. Does she need a new citizenship?
st: India has single citizenship.
She is a citizen of India, not of Kerala alone.
Her rights as an Indian citizen go with her anywhere in India.
So she does not need any new citizenship.
ex.a: No. With single citizenship, she remains an Indian citizen everywhere in India.

topics.rl: When an Indian travels abroad, the Indian passport shows that the person is a citizen of India and can seek help from Indian embassies.

topics.h: Imagine a school with no rules to protect you from bullies. The Fundamental Rights are like the Constitution's protection for every person.
p: Fundamental Rights are listed in Part III of the Constitution. There are six: the Right to Equality, the Right to Freedom, the Right against Exploitation, the Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
The Right to Equality includes equality before the law and the abolition of untouchability (Article 17).

The Right to Freedom includes freedom of speech and expression and the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21). Article 21A gives children aged 6 to 14 the right to free and compulsory education.
The Right against Exploitation bans forced labour and the employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and other hazardous work.
The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) lets citizens go directly to the Supreme Court if their rights are violated. Dr B. R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

ex.q: Think it through: A shop owner keeps a 12-year-old boy working in his hazardous fireworks unit instead of letting him go to school. Which rights are being violated?
st: Children below 14 cannot be employed in hazardous work: Right against Exploitation.
Children aged 6 to 14 have the right to free and compulsory education: Article 21A.
If rights are violated, the matter can be taken to court: Right to Constitutional Remedies.
ex.a: The Right against Exploitation and the right to education (Article 21A); the boy's rights can be protected through the courts.

topics.rl: Children in government schools get free education and textbooks thanks to the right to education in Article 21A, which was added in 2002 and came into force in 2010.

topics.h: Rights are like the keys to a house; duties are like keeping the house clean and safe. A good citizen needs both.
p: Fundamental Duties are listed in Article 51A (Part IVA) of the Constitution. They were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.
There were ten duties at first. The 86th Amendment in 2002 added an eleventh: parents or guardians must provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6 to 14.
Duties include respecting the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem; protecting the unity and integrity of India; and promoting harmony and brotherhood among all people.
Other duties are to protect the natural environment, to develop a scientific temper, to safeguard public property and give up violence, and to strive for excellence in all activities.
Unlike Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties are not directly enforceable in courts, but they remind every citizen of their responsibilities.

ex.q: Think it through: Students on a school trip see others scratching names on an old monument. Which duty is being ignored, and what can the students do?
st: Monuments are part of our heritage and are public property.
Citizens have a duty to value our rich heritage and to safeguard public property.
The students can politely tell the others to stop and inform the guard or teacher.
By doing so, they practise their own Fundamental Duties.
ex.a: The duties to value our heritage and safeguard public property; the students can stop it and inform the authorities.

topics.rl: Standing up for the National Anthem, keeping parks clean and planting trees on Van Mahotsav are simple ways of doing your duties.

topics.h: Every day in India, many thousands of babies are born. Some people pass away and some people move in or out. Together these decide how the population changes.
p: Population changes because of three things: births, deaths and migration (people moving into or out of a place).
The birth rate is the number of live births per 1,000 people in a year. The death rate is the number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year.
The natural growth rate is the birth rate minus the death rate. When births are more than deaths, the population grows.
Better health care, clean water and vaccines lowered death rates, so India's population grew fast in the 20th century. Birth rates have also been falling over time.

India counts its people through the Census, held every ten years. According to the Census of 2011, India had about 121 crore people. United Nations estimates show that India became the world's most populous country in 2023, overtaking China.

ex.q: Think it through: A town has a birth rate of 20 per 1,000 and a death rate of 7 per 1,000. What is its natural growth rate?
st: Natural growth rate = birth rate − death rate.
So the town grows by 13 people per 1,000 each year, not counting migration.
ex.a: 13 per 1,000 people per year.

topics.rl: Census officials visit every home, even in remote villages and islands, to count each person. The data helps the government plan schools, hospitals and roads.

topics.h: Some parts of India are packed with people, while in parts of Ladakh you may travel for hours without seeing a house. Why?
p: Population distribution means how people are spread over an area. In India and the world, it is very uneven.
Population density is the number of people living per square kilometre. Density = total population ÷ area. According to the Census of 2011, India's density was 382 people per sq km.
Physical factors affect distribution: flat land, fertile soil, a pleasant climate and water attract people. Mountains, deserts, thick forests and very cold or very hot places have few people.
Economic and social factors matter too: jobs in industries and cities, minerals, transport, and services like schools and hospitals draw people.

The Ganga plains and coastal plains are densely populated. The Thar Desert, the high Himalayas and Ladakh are thinly populated. In the 2011 Census, Bihar had the highest density among the states and Arunachal Pradesh the lowest.

ex.q: Think it through: A district has 6,00,000 people and an area of 1,500 sq km. What is its population density?
st: Density = population ÷ area.
So 400 people live in each square kilometre on average.
ex.a: 400 people per sq km.

topics.rl: Kolkata, Patna and Lucknow on the fertile Ganga plains are crowded, while hill towns in Arunachal Pradesh are small and spread out.

topics.t: Population composition: people as a resource
topics.h: Two towns have the same number of people. In one, most are children; in the other, most are grandparents. Would their needs be the same?
p: Population composition describes the make-up of a population by age, sex, literacy, occupation and where people live.
By age, people are grouped as children, working-age adults and the elderly. Children and the elderly depend on working-age people.
The sex ratio is the number of females per 1,000 males. According to the Census of 2011, India's sex ratio was 943, and Kerala had the highest among the states.
A population pyramid is a graph that shows how many males and females are in each age group. A wide base means many children.
India has a large share of young people. If they are healthy, educated and skilled, they can become a huge strength for the country. This is called the demographic dividend.

ex.q: Think it through: A village has 450 females and 500 males. What is its sex ratio?
st: Sex ratio = females per 1,000 males.
ex.a: 900 females per 1,000 males.

topics.rl: Programmes like Skill India and the push for girls' education aim to turn India's young population into a skilled workforce.

topics.h: Every morning, lakhs of people pour into Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru by train, bus and metro. Why do so many people move to cities?
p: Urbanisation is the increase in the share of a country's people who live in towns and cities.
Cities grow because people migrate from villages for jobs, education and health care, because of natural growth of the city population, and because villages near cities become part of them.
In India, statutory towns are places with a municipal corporation, municipality, cantonment board or notified town area.
A census town is a place with at least 5,000 people, a density of at least 400 people per sq km, and at least 75% of male main workers doing non-farm work.

Towns and cities are run by urban local bodies: municipal corporations for big cities (headed by a mayor), municipalities for smaller towns, and nagar panchayats for areas changing from rural to urban.

ex.q: Think it through: A place has 8,000 people, a density of 500 per sq km, and 80% of its male main workers do non-farm work. It has no municipality. Is it a census town?
st: Population: 8,000 is at least 5,000. ✔
Density: 500 is at least 400 per sq km. ✔
Non-farm male main workers: 80% is at least 75%. ✔
All three conditions are met.
ex.a: Yes, it is a census town.

topics.rl: When a new metro line or IT park opens near a village, the village often grows into a busy town within a few years.

topics.t: Kinds of cities: old, planned and new
topics.h: Over 4,000 years ago, Harappan cities had straight streets and covered drains. Some modern Indian cities are still planned the same careful way!
p: Cities of the Harappan Civilisation, such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and Lothal, had planned streets in a grid and good drainage.
Many towns grew around a special function: temple towns like Madurai and Puri, port towns like Surat and Kozhikode, and capital cities like Delhi and Fatehpur Sikri.
Jaipur was planned in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, with wide streets in a grid. Its walled city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
During colonial rule, Bombay (Mumbai), Madras (Chennai) and Calcutta (Kolkata) grew as port cities and trade centres.

After independence, new planned cities were built, such as Chandigarh, designed by the architect Le Corbusier. Some cities are known for one main activity, like Jamshedpur for steel and Bengaluru for information technology.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did port towns like Surat and Kozhikode grow into big trading centres?
st: They were on the coast with harbours for ships.
Ships brought goods from other countries and carried Indian goods away.
Traders, workers, sailors and craftspeople came to live there.
Markets, warehouses and services grew, and so did the town.
ex.a: Their harbours made them centres of sea trade, which drew traders and workers and made the towns grow.

topics.rl: Chandigarh is divided into numbered sectors, each planned with its own market, school and park, so people can find addresses easily.

topics.h: Traffic jams, garbage heaps and water tankers: cities give us jobs and comforts, but they also face big problems. Can we fix them?
p: When cities grow faster than housing, many people live in slums with crowded homes and poor water and sanitation.
More vehicles cause traffic jams and air pollution. Public transport like buses and metro rail can carry many people using less road space. India's first metro opened in Kolkata in 1984.
Cities produce huge amounts of waste. Separating wet and dry waste at home, composting and recycling reduce the load on landfills.
Concrete and roads cover the soil, so rainwater cannot soak in. This causes urban flooding and falling groundwater. Rainwater harvesting, lakes and green spaces help.
Cities are often hotter than nearby villages because concrete and asphalt soak up heat. This is called the urban heat island effect. Trees and parks help to cool them.

ex.q: Think it through: Why does a city get flooded after heavy rain even if it is not near a river?
st: Roads, buildings and pavements cover most of the ground.
Rainwater cannot soak into the soil.
Drains get blocked by plastic and waste, or are too small.
So water collects on the roads.
ex.a: Hard surfaces stop rain from soaking in, and blocked or small drains cannot carry it away, so water floods the streets.

topics.rl: Many housing societies now have separate green and blue bins for wet and dry waste, and metro trains in cities like Delhi, Chennai and Kochi carry lakhs of riders daily.

topics.h: A weaver in Varanasi, a princess in Rajasthan and a tailor in Maharashtra all sang songs of devotion that people still sing today. What connected them?
p: Bhakti means loving devotion to God. Bhakti saints taught that sincere love for God mattered more than rituals, and that all people, of every caste and gender, could reach God.
The bhakti tradition began much earlier in the Tamil region with the Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and the Nayanars (devotees of Shiva), and spread across India.
Saints composed in the languages of ordinary people. In Maharashtra, Jnaneshwar (13th century) wrote the Jnaneshwari in Marathi, and Namdev and Tukaram sang of Vithoba of Pandharpur.
In north India, Kabir (15th century) wrote dohas against blind ritual, Mirabai sang of her devotion to Krishna, Surdas wrote in Braj Bhasha, and Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi.
In the east, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu spread Krishna kirtan in Bengal, and Sankaradeva in Assam set up namghars (prayer halls) and sattras (monasteries). Lal Ded composed verses in Kashmiri.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did bhakti saints write in regional languages such as Marathi, Awadhi and Assamese instead of Sanskrit?
st: Most ordinary people did not know Sanskrit.
The saints wanted everyone to understand and sing their songs.
Songs in everyday language spread quickly from village to village.
This also enriched regional literature.
ex.a: So that ordinary people could understand and sing them; this spread their message widely and enriched regional languages.

topics.rl: Lakhs of Varkari pilgrims walk to Pandharpur every year singing abhangas of Tukaram and Jnaneshwar, and Kabir's dohas are still taught in Hindi classes.

topics.t: Sufi saints and the Sikh tradition
topics.h: At the dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi, qawwals sing every Thursday evening, as they have for centuries. Who were the Sufis?
p: Sufis were Muslim mystics who stressed love and devotion to God, simple living and service to all people.

A Sufi teacher (pir or murshid) lived with disciples (murids) in a khanqah, a hospice open to all. The tomb-shrine of a Sufi saint is called a dargah, and the yearly celebration of the saint's death anniversary is called urs.

The Chishti order was very popular in India. Its saints include Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti of Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi and Baba Farid of Punjab. Some verses of Baba Farid are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.
The poet Amir Khusrau, a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, wrote in Persian and Hindavi and is linked with the growth of qawwali, devotional music sung at Sufi gatherings (sama).

Guru Nanak (1469–1539) taught devotion to one God, honest work and sharing. He started the langar, a community kitchen where all eat together. The Adi Granth was compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, and Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699.

ex.q: Think it through: How does a langar express the idea of equality?
st: Everyone, rich or poor, of any caste or religion, is welcome.
All sit together in rows on the floor.
Everyone is served the same simple food.
Volunteers cook and serve as a form of service (seva).
ex.a: By having everyone sit together and eat the same food, with no difference of caste, religion or wealth.

topics.rl: The langar at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar serves free meals to huge numbers of visitors every day, and the urs at Ajmer Sharif draws pilgrims of many faiths.

topics.h: Imagine paintings so tiny and detailed that artists used the finest brushes, some made of squirrel hair! These are miniature paintings.
p: Miniature paintings are small, detailed paintings made on paper, often for books and albums. Mughal emperors kept workshops of painters.
Akbar's painters illustrated the Hamzanama, a book of adventure stories. Under Jahangir, the artist Ustad Mansur became famous for paintings of birds, animals and flowers.
Rajput courts, such as Mewar and Bundi, developed their own painting styles, often showing scenes from the lives of Krishna and Rama and of the seasons.
Literature grew in many languages. Babur wrote his memoirs, the Baburnama, in Turkish; Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama in Persian; and Akbar had the Mahabharata translated into Persian as the Razmnama.

Regional languages flourished too: the Vijayanagara king Krishnadevaraya wrote the Amuktamalyada in Telugu, and Purandara Dasa composed songs in Kannada and is called the father of Carnatic music. Tansen was a famous musician at Akbar's court.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did Akbar have the Mahabharata translated into Persian?
st: Persian was the language of the Mughal court.
Many nobles and officials could read Persian but not Sanskrit.
A translation let them learn the great epic of India.
This fitted his policy of understanding the many traditions of his people.
ex.a: So that the Persian-reading court could understand an important Indian epic, in line with his interest in the traditions of all his subjects.

topics.rl: Museums such as the National Museum in Delhi display Mughal and Rajput miniatures, and Carnatic music students still begin with lessons composed by Purandara Dasa.

qa.q: Which of these is a human-made resource?
qa.e: A cotton mill is built by people. Rivers, coal and sunlight come from nature.

qa.q: What turns a natural substance into a resource?
qa.a: People find a use for it and have the technology to use it
qa.e: Usefulness, value and the means to use something make it a resource.

qa.q: A trained nurse working in a village health centre is an example of a:
qa.e: People with skills and knowledge are human resources.

qa.q: Which pair has only natural resources?
qa.e: Forests and minerals both come from nature without being made by people.

qa.q: Why is investing in education and health important for a country's resources?
qa.a: It improves human resources, the people who use all other resources
qa.e: Skilled and healthy people can use and manage other resources better.

qa.q: Uranium was found in rocks long before it was used to make electricity. When did it become a resource for power?
qa.a: After people developed the technology to use it in nuclear power plants
qa.e: A substance becomes a resource for a purpose once people have the knowledge and technology to use it.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a natural resource?
qa.e: A highway is constructed by people, so it is human-made.

qa.q: A potter shapes clay from a riverbank into pots. The pots are:
qa.a: Human-made resources made from a natural resource
qa.e: Clay is natural; the pots are made by people, so they are human-made resources.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-renewable resource?
qa.e: Natural gas takes millions of years to form, so it cannot be replaced quickly.

qa.q: Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?
qa.a: They take millions of years to form
qa.e: Their formation is so slow that, once used, they are not replaced within human time.

qa.q: Which statement about forests is correct?
qa.a: Forests are renewable but can be destroyed if cut faster than they regrow
qa.e: Trees regrow, but overcutting can wipe out a forest.

qa.q: What were fossil fuels formed from?
qa.a: Remains of plants and animals buried long ago
qa.e: Buried remains changed slowly under heat and pressure into coal, oil and gas.

qa.q: A region has rich coal deposits but little iron ore. What does uneven distribution of resources often lead to?
qa.e: When resources are unevenly spread, regions exchange what they have for what they lack.

qa.q: Which energy source is renewable?
qa.e: The Sun keeps giving light and heat every day.

qa.q: Groundwater is renewed by rain, yet wells in some places are drying up. Why?
qa.a: Water is being pumped out faster than rain can refill it
qa.e: Even a renewable resource runs short if it is used faster than nature renews it.

qa.q: Which group contains only fossil fuels?
qa.e: These three formed underground from ancient remains over millions of years.

qa.q: Which best describes sustainable use of resources?
qa.a: Meeting today's needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
qa.e: Sustainable use balances present needs with the needs of the future.

qa.q: Carrying a cloth bag instead of taking a new plastic bag each time is an example of:
qa.e: You are reducing the number of plastic bags used.

qa.q: Sacred groves found in many parts of India help to:
qa.a: Protect patches of forest and their plants and animals
qa.e: Communities have traditionally protected these groves, keeping trees and wildlife safe.

qa.q: Which practice harms a renewable resource?
qa.a: Pumping groundwater faster than rain can refill it
qa.e: Over-pumping makes water tables fall, even though water is renewable.

qa.q: 'The Earth provides enough to satisfy every man's need, but not every man's greed.' Whose idea is this?
qa.e: This saying is widely credited to Mahatma Gandhi.

qa.q: Old plastic bottles melted and made into new products is an example of:
qa.e: Recycling changes used material into new products.

qa.q: Why is switching to solar power considered good for sustainability?
qa.a: It uses a renewable source and causes less pollution
qa.e: Sunlight is renewable and solar panels do not burn fuel.

qa.q: Riya's family fixes a dripping tap at once. What are they conserving?
qa.e: A dripping tap can waste many litres of water every day.

qa.q: In which year did the Delhi Sultanate begin?
qa.e: Qutb-ud-din Aibak became Sultan in 1206 CE, starting the Delhi Sultanate.

qa.q: Which was the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate?
qa.e: The Lodis ruled last; Ibrahim Lodi lost to Babur in 1526.

qa.q: Who was the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate?
qa.e: Razia, daughter of Iltutmish, ruled from 1236 to 1240 CE.

qa.q: Which Sultan moved his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad?
qa.e: Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted the capital to Daulatabad (Devagiri) in the Deccan.

qa.q: Alauddin Khalji is remembered for:
qa.e: He set fixed prices for goods like grain so that his large army could be paid and fed.

qa.q: Which Central Asian ruler attacked and plundered Delhi in 1398 CE?
qa.e: Timur's attack in 1398 weakened the Delhi Sultanate.

qa.q: Who began building the Qutub Minar in Delhi?
qa.e: Aibak began it and his successor Iltutmish completed it.

qa.q: How many years did the Delhi Sultanate last, from 1206 to 1526?
Who founded the Mughal empire in India?
qa.e: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in 1526 and founded the empire.

qa.q: In which year was the First Battle of Panipat fought?
qa.e: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.

qa.q: Who defeated Humayun and ruled north India for some years?
qa.e: Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun in 1540; Humayun regained his throne in 1555.

qa.q: Akbar's policy of 'sulh-i-kul' meant:
qa.e: Sulh-i-kul means universal peace, respecting people of different faiths.

qa.q: Under which emperor did the Mughal empire reach its largest size?
qa.e: Aurangzeb extended Mughal rule far into the Deccan.

qa.q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal?
qa.e: Shah Jahan built it in Agra in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

qa.q: In a mansab, the rank of an officer decided:
qa.a: His pay and the number of soldiers and horses he kept
qa.e: Rank fixed salary and military duties.

qa.q: Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605. For about how many years did he rule?
Who founded the Vijayanagara empire in 1336?
qa.e: The brothers Harihara and Bukka founded it in 1336.

qa.q: On which river was the city of Vijayanagara (Hampi) located?
qa.e: Hampi stands on the banks of the Tungabhadra in present-day Karnataka.

qa.q: Which battle in 1565 led to the ruin of the Vijayanagara capital?
qa.e: An alliance of Deccan Sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565.

qa.q: Maharana Pratap fought Akbar's army at:
qa.e: The Battle of Haldighati was fought in 1576.

qa.q: Who led the Ahoms to victory at the Battle of Saraighat?
qa.e: Lachit Borphukan defeated the Mughals on the Brahmaputra in 1671.

qa.q: In which year was the Battle of Saraighat fought?
qa.e: It was fought in 1671 near Guwahati.

qa.q: Rani Durgavati ruled the kingdom of:
qa.e: She was the queen of Garha-Katanga in central India.

qa.q: Rana Sanga of Mewar fought Babur at Khanwa in 1527. How many years was this after the First Battle of Panipat (1526)?
Where was Shivaji born?
qa.e: Shivaji was born at Shivneri in 1630.

qa.q: Who was Shivaji's mother?
qa.e: Jijabai raised Shivaji and inspired him.

qa.q: In which year was Shivaji crowned Chhatrapati?
qa.e: His coronation took place at Raigad in 1674.

qa.q: What kind of fighting did Shivaji's soldiers use in the hills?
qa.e: Small groups made surprise attacks using their knowledge of the terrain.

qa.q: Which general of Bijapur did Shivaji defeat at Pratapgad in 1659?
qa.e: Shivaji defeated Afzal Khan at Pratapgad.

qa.q: From whose custody in Agra did Shivaji escape in 1666?
qa.e: Shivaji was held at Aurangzeb's court in Agra and escaped.

qa.q: The Sahyadris, where Shivaji built his forts, are also called:
qa.e: The Sahyadri range is the Western Ghats.

qa.q: Shivaji was born in 1630 and crowned in 1674. How old was he at his coronation (about)?
What was the Ashtapradhan?
qa.e: Ashta means eight; pradhan means minister.

qa.q: Who was the chief minister in the Ashtapradhan?
qa.e: The Peshwa was the chief minister; the Senapati was the army chief.

qa.q: Chauth was a tax equal to what share of the revenue?
qa.e: Chauth comes from the word for 'fourth'.

qa.q: Sardeshmukhi was an extra tax of:
qa.e: Sardeshmukhi was an additional 10% of the revenue.

qa.q: Why did Shivaji build a navy?
qa.a: To protect the coast and sea trade
qa.e: The Konkan coast faced threats from foreign and coastal powers.

qa.q: Sindhudurg is an example of:
qa.e: It was built on an island off the Konkan coast.

qa.q: Why did Shivaji prefer paying many soldiers in cash rather than land?
qa.a: So they stayed loyal to the state, not to their own estates
qa.e: Land grants could make officers independent; cash pay kept them dependent on the state.

qa.q: A region's revenue is ₹2,000. What is the chauth on it?
qa.e: Chauth = one-fourth: 2000 ÷ 4 = 500.

qa.q: Who were the real leaders of the Maratha state for most of the 18th century?
qa.e: The Peshwas, based in Pune, led the Maratha state.

qa.q: Which Peshwa led Maratha armies deep into north India in the 1720s and 1730s?
qa.e: Bajirao I was famous for his fast cavalry campaigns northwards.

qa.q: Against whom did the Marathas fight the Third Battle of Panipat?
qa.e: Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) of Afghanistan defeated them in 1761.

qa.q: The Scindia family ruled from:
qa.e: The Scindias (Shindes) made Gwalior their centre.

qa.q: Ahilyabai Holkar is best remembered for:
qa.a: Good administration and building temples, ghats and wells
qa.e: She ruled from Maheshwar and is admired for her wise, caring rule.

qa.q: Which battle did the Marathas lose in 1761?
qa.e: The Third Battle of Panipat was fought on 14 January 1761.

qa.q: Which statement about the Maratha confederacy is correct?
qa.a: Several Maratha chiefs ruled their own regions under the Peshwa's leadership
qa.e: Holkars, Scindias, Gaekwads and Bhonsles ruled regions while accepting the Peshwa as head.

qa.q: Shivaji died in 1680 and the Third Battle of Panipat was in 1761. How many years apart were these?
Who reached Calicut by sea from Europe in 1498?
qa.e: The Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama opened the sea route to India.

qa.q: In which year did the English East India Company get its royal charter?
qa.e: Queen Elizabeth I granted the charter in 1600.

qa.q: What were the trading posts of European companies called?
qa.e: A 'factory' then meant a trading post where agents (factors) stored and traded goods.

qa.q: Which goods drew European traders to India?
