qa.a: Spices and cotton and silk cloth
qa.e: Pepper, cloves, fine cotton and silk cloth were highly prized in Europe.

qa.q: Fort William was the Company's fort in:
qa.e: Fort William was in Calcutta (Kolkata); Fort St George was in Madras.

qa.q: Which European power did the English fight in south India in the 18th century?
qa.e: The English and French companies fought several wars for control in the south.

qa.q: Which queen gave the English East India Company its charter?
qa.e: Elizabeth I granted it in 1600; Victoria became Empress of India much later.

qa.q: Calicut, where Vasco da Gama landed, is on the coast of which present-day state?
qa.e: Calicut (Kozhikode) is on the Malabar coast of Kerala.

qa.q: Who won the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
qa.a: Robert Clive and the East India Company
qa.e: Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal, helped by Mir Jafar's betrayal.

qa.q: What did the Company receive in 1765?
qa.a: The Diwani of Bengal (right to collect revenue)
qa.e: After Buxar, Shah Alam II granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company.

qa.q: In which year was the Battle of Buxar fought?
qa.e: Buxar (1764) came seven years after Plassey.

qa.q: Who was the ruler of Mysore who died fighting the Company in 1799?
qa.e: Tipu Sultan died defending his capital Srirangapatna.

qa.q: The Doctrine of Lapse was introduced by:
qa.e: Dalhousie used it to take over kingdoms without a natural male heir.

qa.q: Where did the Revolt of 1857 begin on 10 May?
qa.e: Sepoys at Meerut rose first and then marched to Delhi.

qa.q: What change came after the Revolt of 1857?
qa.a: The British Crown took over rule of India from the Company
qa.e: In 1858 the British Parliament ended Company rule and the Crown ruled directly.

qa.q: How many years after Plassey (1757) was the Battle of Buxar (1764)?
Who introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal in 1793?
qa.e: Cornwallis fixed the land revenue that zamindars had to pay.

qa.q: Why did many Indian weavers lose their work during colonial rule?
qa.a: Cheap machine-made cloth from Britain flooded Indian markets
qa.e: Factory cloth was cheaper, and Indian cloth faced high duties in Britain.

qa.q: Who explained the idea of the 'drain of wealth'?
qa.e: Naoroji showed how wealth flowed from India to Britain.

qa.q: Between which places did the first passenger train in India run in 1853?
qa.e: The first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane.

qa.q: Indigo was grown mainly to make:
qa.e: Indigo plants gave a blue dye prized by European textile makers.

qa.q: Which famine of the 18th century caused great suffering in Bengal?
qa.e: The Bengal famine of 1770 came soon after the Company got the Diwani.

qa.q: What was the main purpose of the early railways built by the British?
qa.a: To carry raw materials to ports and British goods inland
qa.e: They mainly served British trade, though Indians also used them.

qa.q: Which is a balanced statement about English education in colonial India?
qa.a: It served British needs, but educated Indians also used it to spread ideas of reform and freedom
qa.e: It trained clerks for the British, yet it also helped Indians read about liberty and organise.

qa.q: What does 'franchise' mean in civics?
qa.e: In elections, franchise means the right to vote.

qa.q: What is the minimum age to vote in India?
qa.e: Since the 61st Amendment (1988), citizens aged 18 or above can vote.

qa.q: Which amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18?
qa.e: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act of 1988 made the change.

qa.q: When were India's first general elections held?
qa.e: They were held from October 1951 to early 1952.

qa.q: Universal adult franchise means:
qa.a: All adult citizens can vote regardless of caste, religion, gender or wealth
qa.e: 'Universal' means for all adults, without discrimination.

qa.q: Why were party symbols printed on ballots in early elections?
qa.a: So that voters who could not read could identify their choice
qa.e: Symbols made voting possible for everyone, literate or not.

qa.q: Which country gave women the right to vote in national elections only in 1971?
qa.e: Swiss women got the federal vote in 1971; India gave it to women from the start in 1950.

qa.q: What does 'one person, one vote, one value' mean?
qa.a: Every voter has one vote and every vote counts equally
qa.e: It is the principle of political equality.

qa.q: When was the Election Commission of India set up?
qa.e: It was set up a day before the Constitution came into force.

qa.q: Which article of the Constitution deals with the Election Commission?
qa.e: Article 324 gives the Commission power over elections.

qa.q: Who was India's first Chief Election Commissioner?
qa.e: Sukumar Sen conducted the first general elections in 1951–52.

qa.q: National Voters' Day is celebrated on:
qa.e: It marks the founding day of the Election Commission.

qa.q: Who conducts elections to gram panchayats?
qa.e: Local body elections are conducted by State Election Commissions.

qa.q: What is the Model Code of Conduct?
qa.a: A set of rules that parties and candidates must follow during elections
qa.e: It guides speeches, campaigns and use of government resources during elections.

qa.q: Why must the Election Commission be independent?
qa.a: So that it treats all parties equally and elections stay fair
qa.e: Independence keeps the referee neutral.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a job of the Election Commission of India?
qa.e: Laws are made by Parliament; the Commission conducts elections.

qa.q: What is a constituency?
qa.a: An area whose voters elect one representative
qa.e: Each constituency elects one member to the Lok Sabha or the Assembly.

qa.q: How many Lok Sabha constituencies are there?
qa.e: 543 members of the Lok Sabha are elected from 543 constituencies.

qa.q: What is the minimum age to contest a Lok Sabha election?
qa.e: Candidates must be at least 25; for the Rajya Sabha it is 30.

qa.q: What does a VVPAT do?
qa.a: Shows a paper slip so the voter can check the vote cast
qa.e: VVPAT stands for Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail.

qa.q: Why is indelible ink put on a voter's finger?
qa.a: To prevent the same person from voting twice
qa.e: The ink cannot be washed off quickly, so it marks who has voted.

qa.q: In a constituency, P gets 40,000 votes, Q gets 38,000 and R gets 22,000. Under first-past-the-post, who wins?
qa.e: P has the most votes, so P wins, even without more than half.

qa.q: What does NOTA allow a voter to do?
qa.a: Show that they do not want to vote for any of the candidates
qa.e: NOTA means 'None of the Above'. It records that the voter chose none of the candidates; the candidate with the most votes still wins.

qa.q: Why are some constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
qa.a: To make sure these communities are fairly represented
qa.e: Only candidates from these groups can contest there, though all voters vote.

qa.q: Which three parts make up the Parliament of India?
qa.a: President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
qa.e: The President is a part of Parliament, though not a member of either House.

qa.q: Who presides over the Lok Sabha?
qa.e: The Speaker is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha.

qa.q: Who is the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
qa.e: The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

qa.q: How many members of the Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President?
qa.e: The President nominates 12 members with special knowledge of art, literature, science or social service.

qa.q: What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member?
qa.e: Members serve six years; one-third retire every two years.

qa.q: Who elects most members of the Rajya Sabha?
qa.a: Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
qa.e: This indirect election lets the states be represented.

qa.q: Which House is called the 'House of the People'?
qa.e: 'Lok' means people; its members are directly elected.

qa.q: How many more members are elected to the Lok Sabha (543) than the maximum size of the Rajya Sabha (250)?
What is a bill?
qa.e: A bill is a draft law placed before Parliament.

qa.q: After both Houses pass a bill, who must give assent before it becomes law?
qa.e: The President's assent turns a bill into an Act.

qa.q: Where can a Money Bill be introduced?
qa.e: Money Bills start only in the Lok Sabha, the directly elected House.

qa.q: Within how many days must the Rajya Sabha return a Money Bill?
qa.e: The Rajya Sabha can suggest changes but must return it within 14 days.

qa.q: What happens during Question Hour?
qa.a: Members ask ministers questions about the government's work
qa.e: It helps Parliament keep the government answerable.

qa.q: Once a bill becomes law, it is called:
qa.e: An enacted bill is called an Act, such as the Right to Education Act.

qa.q: Which is a main job of Parliament?
qa.a: Making laws and keeping a check on the government
qa.e: Parliament is the legislature: it makes laws and holds the executive accountable.

qa.q: Who can introduce an ordinary bill in Parliament?
qa.a: A minister or any member of Parliament
qa.e: Bills by ministers are government bills; those by other members are private members' bills.

qa.q: Who is the head of the government in India?
qa.e: The President is head of the State; the Prime Minister leads the government.

qa.q: Who appoints the Prime Minister?
qa.e: The President appoints the leader who has majority support in the Lok Sabha.

qa.q: To which House is the Council of Ministers collectively responsible?
qa.e: The government stays in office only while it has the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

qa.q: Who elects the President of India?
qa.a: An electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs
qa.e: Elected members of both Houses and of State Legislative Assemblies vote.

qa.q: What happens if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the government?
qa.a: The Council of Ministers must resign
qa.e: Losing the House's confidence ends the government.

qa.q: The Cabinet is made up of:
qa.a: Senior ministers led by the Prime Minister
qa.e: The Cabinet is the inner group of the Council of Ministers.

qa.q: Which group forms the permanent executive?
qa.a: Civil servants such as IAS officers
qa.e: Civil servants stay in service even when governments change.

qa.q: In the parliamentary system, the executive:
qa.a: Comes from the legislature and is answerable to it
qa.e: Ministers are members of Parliament and answer to it.

qa.q: Which of these is 'land' as a factor of production?
qa.e: In economics, land means all natural resources.

qa.q: The payment received for the use of land is called:
qa.e: Rent is the reward for land.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of labour?
qa.e: Labour is human effort, physical or mental.

qa.q: What is the payment for labour called?
qa.e: Wages (or salaries) are paid for labour.

qa.q: Which statement about land is correct?
qa.a: Its total quantity is limited and cannot be increased
qa.e: Land is a gift of nature and its total supply is fixed.

qa.q: Education, training and health that make workers more productive are called:
qa.e: Investing in people makes their labour more valuable.

qa.q: Mental effort, like an architect planning a building, counts as:
qa.e: Labour includes both physical and mental work.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a factor of production?
qa.e: The four factors are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.

qa.q: Which of these is fixed capital?
qa.e: A loom is used again and again for years.

qa.q: Which of these is working capital?
qa.e: Flour is used up in making bread, so it is working capital.

qa.q: The reward for capital is called:
qa.e: Interest is paid for the use of money capital.

qa.q: How is capital different from land?
qa.a: Capital is made by people; land is a gift of nature
qa.e: Tools and machines are produced by humans; natural resources are not.

qa.q: Why is a tractor called fixed capital even though it moves?
qa.a: It is used again and again over many years
qa.e: 'Fixed' refers to long-lasting use, not to being unable to move.

qa.q: A farmer buys seeds, fertiliser and a water pump. Which is fixed capital?
qa.e: The pump lasts many seasons; the others are used up.

qa.q: Raw materials and money in hand are called:
qa.e: They circulate and get used up during production.

qa.q: A shopkeeper borrows ₹10,000 and must pay back ₹11,000 after a year. How much interest does he pay?
qa.e: Interest = amount paid back − amount borrowed = 11,000 − 10,000 = 1,000.

qa.q: Who organises land, labour and capital to produce goods?
qa.e: The entrepreneur brings the factors together and takes decisions.

qa.q: What is the reward for entrepreneurship?
qa.e: Profit is what remains after all costs are paid.

qa.q: Why is an entrepreneur called a risk-taker?
qa.a: They may face a loss if the business does not succeed
qa.e: Unlike a worker on fixed wages, the entrepreneur bears profit or loss.

qa.q: A juice seller earns ₹3,000 and spends ₹2,200 on fruit, rent and a helper's wages. What is his profit?
Introducing a new product or a better way of making it is called:
qa.e: Innovation is a key quality of entrepreneurs.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of entrepreneurship?
qa.a: A woman starts a tailoring unit and hires two workers
qa.e: Starting and running the unit, and bearing risk, is entrepreneurship.

qa.q: Which list correctly gives all four factors of production?
qa.e: Rent, wages, interest and profit are the rewards, not the factors.

qa.q: How do entrepreneurs help an economy?
qa.a: They create jobs and bring new goods and services
qa.e: New businesses employ people and meet needs in new ways.

qa.q: How many continents are there?
qa.e: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.

qa.q: Which is the largest continent?
qa.e: Asia is the largest in area and population.

qa.q: Which is the largest ocean?
qa.e: The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean.

qa.q: Which continent is crossed by the Equator and both the Tropics?
qa.e: The Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn all pass through Africa.

qa.q: Which ocean is named after a country?
qa.e: It is the only ocean named after a country, India.

qa.q: Maitri and Bharati are Indian research stations in:
qa.e: India runs these stations in Antarctica.

qa.q: Which is the smallest ocean?
qa.e: The Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, is the smallest.

qa.q: In which part of Asia is India located?
qa.e: India lies in South Asia, with the Himalayas to the north and the Indian Ocean to the south.

qa.q: The temperate grasslands of North America are called:
qa.e: The Prairies stretch across the USA and Canada.

qa.q: The Pampas are found in:
qa.e: The Pampas lie mainly in Argentina.

qa.q: The Steppes stretch across:
qa.e: They extend from eastern Europe across Central Asia.

qa.q: Which animal is commonly found in the African savanna?
qa.e: Zebras graze on the tall grasses of the savanna.

qa.q: The Veld is a grassland of:
qa.e: The Veld is in southern Africa.

qa.q: What kind of plants grow in the tundra?
qa.e: Frozen ground and a short summer allow only small plants.

qa.q: Why are temperate grasslands major wheat-growing areas?
qa.a: They have flat land, fertile soil and moderate rainfall
qa.e: These conditions suit grain crops and farm machines.

qa.q: The temperate grasslands of Australia are called:
qa.e: The Downs are in south-eastern Australia.

qa.q: Which is the highest mountain range in the world?
qa.e: The Himalayas contain Mount Everest and many of the world's highest peaks.

qa.q: Which is the longest mountain range on land?
qa.e: The Andes run along the western side of South America.

qa.q: Mount Everest lies on the border of:
qa.e: Everest is on the Nepal–China (Tibet) border.

qa.q: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
qa.e: The Sahara covers much of northern Africa.

qa.q: The Gobi is an example of:
qa.e: The Gobi in Mongolia and China has very cold winters.

qa.q: Which river carries the most water in the world?
qa.e: The Amazon has the largest flow of water of any river.

qa.q: Where is the Great Barrier Reef?
qa.a: Off the north-eastern coast of Australia
qa.e: It is the world's largest coral reef system.

qa.q: Who was the first Indian woman to climb Mount Everest?
qa.e: Bachendri Pal reached the summit in 1984.

qa.q: When was the Indian National Congress founded?
qa.e: It was founded in December 1885 at Bombay.

qa.q: Where was the first session of the Indian National Congress held?
qa.e: The first session met in Bombay in December 1885.

qa.q: Who presided over the first session of the Congress?
qa.e: W. C. Bonnerjee was its first president.

qa.q: Who said 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'?
qa.e: Tilak made this declaration famous.

qa.q: Which event of 1905 led to the Swadeshi movement?
qa.e: Lord Curzon's partition of Bengal sparked boycotts and swadeshi.

qa.q: What did 'swadeshi' encourage people to do?
qa.a: Use goods made in India and boycott British goods
qa.e: Swadeshi means 'of one's own country'.

qa.q: Leaders like Gokhale and Naoroji, who used petitions and speeches, are called:
qa.e: They believed in gradual reform through peaceful appeals.

qa.q: The partition of Bengal took place in 1905 and was cancelled in 1911. How many years did it last?
When did Mahatma Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
qa.e: He returned in January 1915.

qa.q: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India was for indigo farmers at:
qa.e: Champaran in Bihar, in 1917.

qa.q: On which date did the Jallianwala Bagh incident take place?
qa.e: Troops under General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd in Amritsar on 13 April 1919.

qa.q: Why did Gandhi withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?
qa.a: Because of violence at Chauri Chaura
qa.e: Gandhi insisted the movement must stay non-violent.

qa.q: What did 'Purna Swaraj', demanded in 1929, mean?
qa.e: Purna means 'complete'; Swaraj means 'self-rule'.

qa.q: The Salt March went from Sabarmati Ashram to:
qa.e: Gandhi walked to Dandi on the Gujarat coast, reaching it on 6 April 1930.

qa.q: Which movement was launched on 8 August 1942 with the call 'Do or Die'?
qa.e: Gandhi gave this call in Bombay at the launch of the Quit India Movement.

qa.q: How many years passed between the Salt March (1930) and the Quit India Movement (1942)?
Which leader gave the call 'Dilli Chalo'?
qa.e: Netaji gave this call to the soldiers of the INA.

qa.q: Who led the Bardoli satyagraha of 1928?
qa.e: The success at Bardoli earned him the title 'Sardar'.

qa.q: Who played the key role in uniting the princely states with India after independence?
qa.e: Patel, as Home Minister, persuaded the princely states to join India.

qa.q: On which date were Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru hanged?
qa.e: 23 March is remembered as Shaheed Diwas.

qa.q: Who was the first Indian woman to preside over the Indian National Congress?
qa.e: Sarojini Naidu presided over the Congress session of 1925.

qa.q: Who was the first Prime Minister of independent India?
qa.e: Nehru became Prime Minister on 15 August 1947.

qa.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constitution?
qa.e: Dr Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

qa.q: India became independent in 1947. How many years after the founding of the Congress (1885) was this?
What is the garbhagriha of a temple?
qa.a: The inner sanctum where the main deity is placed
qa.e: Garbhagriha means 'womb chamber', the heart of the temple.

qa.q: A curved tower called a shikhara is typical of which style?
qa.e: Nagara temples of north India have curved shikharas.

qa.q: Who built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur?
qa.e: The Chola king Rajaraja I completed it around 1010 CE.

qa.q: Large gateway towers at the entrance of south Indian temples are called:
qa.e: Gopurams are a key feature of the Dravida style.

qa.q: The Vesara style is a blend of:
qa.e: Vesara combines features of the northern and southern styles.

qa.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora is special because:
qa.a: It was carved out of a single rock
qa.e: Artisans cut it from the top downwards out of one huge rock.

qa.q: The Sun Temple at Konark is in which state?
qa.e: Konark is near Puri in Odisha.

qa.q: The Khajuraho temples were built by the:
qa.e: The Chandela rulers built them in present-day Madhya Pradesh.

qa.q: What is the arcuate method of building?
qa.e: Arcuate comes from 'arc', meaning arch.

qa.q: Who completed the Qutub Minar?
qa.e: Qutb-ud-din Aibak began it and Iltutmish completed it.

qa.q: The Buland Darwaza is at:
qa.e: Akbar built it at his city of Fatehpur Sikri.

qa.q: The Gol Gumbaz, famous for its huge dome, is in:
qa.e: It was built by the Adil Shahi rulers of Bijapur.

qa.q: Humayun's Tomb is set in a charbagh, which is:
qa.a: A garden divided into four parts
qa.e: Char means four; bagh means garden.

qa.q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort in Delhi?
qa.e: Shah Jahan was a great builder.

qa.q: Golconda fort is near which city?
qa.e: Golconda stands on the western side of Hyderabad.

qa.q: Why were arches and domes useful to builders?
qa.a: They could cover wide spaces without many pillars
qa.e: An arch spreads weight to its sides, so wide halls became possible.

qa.q: What is a stupa?
qa.a: A dome-shaped mound built over relics
qa.e: Stupas enshrine relics of the Buddha or Buddhist saints.

qa.q: The Great Stupa at Sanchi was first built in the time of:
qa.e: It dates back to Ashoka's reign in the 3rd century BCE.

qa.q: In rock-cut caves, a chaitya was:
qa.e: Chaityas were halls for worship; viharas were monasteries.

qa.q: Which caves are especially famous for wall paintings?
qa.e: The Ajanta murals are among the finest ancient paintings.

qa.q: Rani ki Vav is a stepwell in:
qa.e: It was built in the 11th century at Patan.

qa.q: The Harmandir Sahib is in:
qa.e: The Golden Temple is in Amritsar, Punjab.

qa.q: The Gateway of India in Mumbai is an example of which style?
qa.e: Built in the colonial period, it mixes Indian and European features.

qa.q: The carved stone gateways of the Sanchi Stupa are called:
qa.e: The four toranas at Sanchi are covered with carved stories.

qa.q: Which is the highest court in India?
qa.e: The Supreme Court is at the top of the judicial pyramid.

qa.q: When was the Supreme Court of India set up?
qa.e: It began functioning two days after the Constitution came into force.

qa.q: Who heads the Supreme Court?
qa.e: The Chief Justice of India leads the Supreme Court.

qa.q: What is an appeal?
qa.a: Asking a higher court to review a lower court's decision
qa.e: Appeals let higher courts correct possible mistakes.

qa.q: What does 'independence of the judiciary' mean?
qa.a: Judges decide cases without pressure from the government or others
qa.e: Independence lets courts protect citizens' rights fairly.

qa.q: The power of courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution is called:
qa.e: Judicial review makes the Constitution supreme.

qa.q: Why is India's judiciary called 'integrated'?
qa.a: Courts at all levels are linked, with the Supreme Court at the top
qa.e: Decisions of higher courts guide all lower courts.

qa.q: Where is the Supreme Court of India located?
qa.e: It sits in New Delhi.

qa.q: What does the 'rule of law' mean?
qa.a: Laws apply equally to everyone and no one is above the law
qa.e: Everyone, from citizens to the government, is bound by law.

qa.q: Which article of the Constitution guarantees equality before the law?
qa.e: Article 14 promises equality before the law and equal protection of the laws.

qa.q: A famous film star breaks a traffic rule. Under the rule of law, what should happen?
qa.a: The same rules and penalties apply as for anyone else
qa.e: Fame gives no exemption from the law.

qa.q: Who upholds the rule of law by applying laws fairly in disputes?
qa.e: Courts interpret and apply the law.

qa.q: Can a citizen challenge an action of the government in court?
qa.a: Yes, if the action is against the law or the Constitution
qa.e: The government also has to act according to the law.

qa.q: Which of these goes against the rule of law?
qa.a: An official refusing to follow a court order because he is powerful
qa.e: Ignoring the law because of power is the opposite of the rule of law.

qa.q: Why is the rule of law important for ordinary people?
qa.a: It protects them from unfair actions by the powerful
qa.e: Equal laws give everyone protection.

qa.q: Which is a feature of fair laws under the rule of law?
qa.a: They are made by the proper process and are known to the public
qa.e: Laws must be clear, public and properly made.

qa.q: Which of these is a criminal case?
qa.e: Theft is a crime; the others are civil disputes.

qa.q: In a criminal case, what is usually filed first with the police?
qa.e: An FIR records the complaint about a crime.

qa.q: What is Public Interest Litigation (PIL)?
qa.a: A case filed by any person or group on behalf of people whose rights are violated
qa.e: PIL opened the courts to those who could not approach them themselves.

qa.q: Which article of the Constitution directs the State to provide free legal aid?
qa.e: Article 39A aims at equal justice and free legal aid.

qa.q: Lok Adalats settle disputes:
qa.a: Quickly, by mutual agreement and with no court fee
qa.e: They are people's courts that encourage compromise.

qa.q: What does 'justice delayed is justice denied' mean?
qa.a: If justice takes too long, it loses much of its value
qa.e: Long delays can cause real harm to people waiting for justice.

qa.q: A poor farmer needs a lawyer but cannot pay. What can he do?
qa.a: Ask the Legal Services Authority for free legal aid
qa.e: Free legal aid is available to those who cannot afford a lawyer.

qa.q: Which of these is a civil case?
qa.a: A dispute over who owns a piece of land
qa.e: Ownership disputes are civil matters between parties.

qa.q: What is a citizen?
qa.a: A full member of a country with rights and duties
qa.e: Citizens are legally members of the nation.

qa.q: Which law governs citizenship in India, along with the Constitution?
qa.e: The Citizenship Act, 1955 lays down how citizenship is acquired.

qa.q: India has:
qa.e: Indians are citizens of the whole country.

qa.q: Which of these is a way of acquiring Indian citizenship?
qa.e: Birth, descent, registration and naturalisation are the ways.

qa.q: Which right is available only to citizens of India?
qa.e: Some rights apply to all persons, but voting is for citizens only.

qa.q: Which office can be held only by a citizen?
qa.e: High constitutional offices are reserved for citizens.

qa.q: Citizenship is described as a 'two-way bond' because:
qa.a: The nation protects our rights and we perform our duties
qa.e: Rights and duties go together.

qa.q: Which is NOT a way of becoming an Indian citizen under the law?
qa.a: Living in India as a tourist for a week
qa.e: A short visit does not give citizenship.

qa.q: How many Fundamental Rights are there in the Indian Constitution now?
qa.e: There are six; the Right to Property was removed in 1978.

qa.q: Which article abolishes untouchability?
qa.e: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice.

qa.q: Which right did Dr Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
qa.e: Without remedies, other rights could not be protected.

qa.q: The right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 is in:
qa.e: Article 21A was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002.

qa.q: Which right bans forced labour?
qa.e: It protects people from forced labour and trafficking.

qa.q: Which right was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights in 1978?
qa.e: The 44th Amendment made it a legal right instead.

qa.q: If a citizen's Fundamental Rights are violated, they can go directly to:
qa.e: Article 32 lets them approach the Supreme Court directly.

qa.q: Freedom of speech and expression is part of which Fundamental Right?
qa.e: The Right to Freedom covers speech, assembly, movement and more.

qa.q: In which article are the Fundamental Duties listed?
qa.e: They are in Article 51A in Part IVA.

qa.q: Which amendment added the Fundamental Duties to the Constitution?
qa.e: The 42nd Amendment added ten duties in 1976.

qa.q: How many Fundamental Duties are there now?
qa.e: There were ten, and the eleventh was added in 2002.

qa.q: Which committee recommended adding Fundamental Duties?
qa.e: The Swaran Singh Committee made the recommendation in 1976.

qa.q: The eleventh duty, added in 2002, is about:
qa.a: Parents providing education to children aged 6 to 14
qa.e: It matches the right to education in Article 21A.

qa.q: Which of these is a Fundamental Duty?
qa.e: Protecting forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife is a duty.

qa.q: How are Fundamental Duties different from Fundamental Rights?
qa.a: Duties are not directly enforceable in courts
qa.e: Rights can be enforced through courts; duties are mainly moral responsibilities.

qa.q: Riya questions superstitions and checks facts before believing them. Which duty is she following?
qa.e: A scientific temper means reasoning and inquiry.

qa.q: Which three factors change the population of a place?
qa.e: People are added by births and in-migration and lost by deaths and out-migration.

qa.q: The birth rate is the number of live births per:
qa.e: Birth rate is measured per 1,000 people per year.

qa.q: A village has a birth rate of 24 and a death rate of 9 per 1,000. What is its natural growth rate per 1,000?
How often is the Census held in India?
qa.e: The Census is held once in ten years.

qa.q: According to the Census of 2011, India's population was about:
qa.e: The 2011 Census counted about 121 crore (1.21 billion) people.

qa.q: Which country did India overtake in 2023 to become the most populous, according to UN estimates?
qa.e: UN estimates show India passed China in 2023.

qa.q: Why did India's population grow quickly in the 20th century?
qa.a: Death rates fell sharply due to better health care, while birth rates stayed high for long
qa.e: Falling deaths with high births cause rapid growth.

qa.q: When people move out of a village to a city for work, the village population changes because of:
qa.e: Out-migration reduces the population of the village.

qa.q: What is population density?
qa.a: The number of people per square kilometre
qa.e: Density tells how crowded a place is.

qa.q: A town has 50,000 people in an area of 100 sq km. What is its density in people per sq km?
According to the Census of 2011, India's population density in people per sq km was:
qa.e: India had 382 people per sq km in 2011.

qa.q: Which region of India is densely populated?
qa.e: Fertile soil, water and flat land attract many people.

qa.q: Why do few people live in the Thar Desert?
qa.a: There is little water and the climate is very harsh
qa.e: Lack of water limits farming and settlement.

qa.q: In the 2011 Census, which state had the lowest population density?
qa.e: Its steep hills and thick forests support few people per sq km.

qa.q: Which of these is an economic factor that attracts people to a place?
qa.e: People move to where they can find work.

qa.q: Region A has 2,000 people on 10 sq km. Region B has 3,000 people on 30 sq km. Which is more densely populated?
What does the sex ratio measure?
qa.a: The number of females per 1,000 males
qa.e: India measures sex ratio as females per 1,000 males.

qa.q: According to the Census of 2011, India's sex ratio was:
qa.e: There were 943 females per 1,000 males in 2011.

qa.q: Which state had the highest sex ratio in the 2011 Census?
qa.e: Kerala had more females than males.

qa.q: A town has 960 females and 1,000 males. What is its sex ratio?
qa.e: 960 females per 1,000 males gives a sex ratio of 960.

qa.q: A population pyramid with a very wide base shows:
qa.e: The base of the pyramid shows the youngest age groups.

qa.q: Which group is usually called 'dependent'?
qa.e: They usually depend on working-age people for support.

qa.q: What is the 'demographic dividend'?
qa.a: The benefit a country can gain from a large, skilled working-age population
qa.e: Young, skilled workers can boost the economy.

qa.q: Why does a population with many children need more schools?
qa.a: Children need education, so demand for schools rises
qa.e: Composition tells planners what services are needed.

qa.q: What is urbanisation?
qa.a: The increase in the share of people living in towns and cities
qa.e: It is the shift of population towards urban areas.

qa.q: What is the minimum population for a census town?
qa.e: A census town needs at least 5,000 people, among other conditions.

qa.q: What minimum density (people per sq km) is required for a census town?
qa.e: The density must be at least 400 per sq km.

qa.q: Which of these is a major reason people move from villages to cities?
qa.a: Jobs and better services like schools and hospitals
qa.e: Cities offer more work in industries and services.

qa.q: Large cities are governed by:
qa.e: Municipal corporations look after big cities.

qa.q: Who heads a municipal corporation?
qa.e: The mayor is the head of a municipal corporation.

qa.q: A place has a municipality. What type of town is it?
qa.e: Statutory towns have a municipal body set up by law.

qa.q: A census town needs at least what percentage of male main workers in non-farm work?
qa.e: At least 75% of male main workers must work outside agriculture.

qa.q: Which feature was typical of Harappan cities?
qa.e: Harappan cities were carefully planned with grid streets and drains.

qa.q: Who designed the city of Chandigarh?
qa.e: The Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier planned Chandigarh.

qa.q: Who planned the city of Jaipur in 1727?
qa.e: Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur as a planned city.

qa.q: Madurai and Puri are examples of:
qa.e: They grew around famous temples.

qa.q: Jamshedpur is best known for:
qa.e: Jamshedpur grew around a large steel plant.

qa.q: During colonial rule, Bombay, Madras and Calcutta grew mainly as:
qa.e: Their ports linked India's trade with the world.

qa.q: Which of these is a Harappan city in Gujarat?
qa.e: Dholavira in Kutch and Lothal are Harappan sites in Gujarat.

qa.q: Bengaluru is often called India's IT hub because:
qa.a: Many information technology companies are based there
qa.e: Thousands of IT firms and startups work from Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why do slums often grow in cities?
qa.a: Cities grow faster than affordable housing
qa.e: Migrants who cannot afford homes settle in crowded areas.

qa.q: Which city had India's first metro rail, opened in 1984?
qa.e: The Kolkata Metro began in 1984; Delhi's opened in 2002.

qa.q: Why does public transport reduce traffic and pollution?
qa.a: One bus or metro train carries many people using less road space
qa.e: Fewer private vehicles mean less congestion and fewer exhaust fumes.

qa.q: What is the urban heat island effect?
qa.a: Cities being hotter than nearby rural areas
qa.e: Concrete and asphalt absorb heat and release it slowly.

qa.q: Which is wet waste?
qa.e: Wet waste is kitchen and food waste that can be composted.

qa.q: Why do many cities face urban flooding?
qa.a: Hard surfaces stop rainwater from soaking in and drains get blocked
qa.e: Concrete surfaces and blocked drains leave water on roads.

qa.q: Which action helps to recharge groundwater in cities?
qa.e: Rainwater harvesting stores rain and lets it soak into the ground.

qa.q: Which is the best way a family can reduce the garbage sent to landfills?
qa.a: Separate wet and dry waste and compost the wet waste
qa.e: Segregation lets wet waste be composted and dry waste be recycled.

qa.q: What does 'bhakti' mean?
qa.e: Bhakti is personal, loving devotion to God.

qa.q: Who were the Nayanars?
qa.e: The Nayanars were devotees of Shiva; the Alvars of Vishnu.

qa.q: Who wrote the Jnaneshwari in Marathi?
qa.e: Jnaneshwar wrote it in the 13th century.

qa.q: Kabir was a weaver who lived in:
qa.e: Kabir lived in Varanasi in the 15th century.

qa.q: Mirabai's songs express her devotion to:
qa.e: Mirabai, a Rajput princess, devoted her songs to Krishna.

qa.q: In which language did Tulsidas write the Ramcharitmanas?
qa.e: He wrote it in Awadhi, a language of the common people.

qa.q: Who set up namghars and sattras in Assam?
qa.e: Sankaradeva spread devotion to Vishnu-Krishna in Assam.

qa.q: Which idea was common to most bhakti saints?
qa.a: Sincere devotion matters more than rituals, and all people can reach God
qa.e: They stressed devotion and equality.

qa.q: Who were the Sufis?
qa.a: Muslim mystics who stressed love and devotion to God
qa.e: Sufis sought closeness to God through love and devotion.

qa.q: The dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti is in:
qa.e: His dargah at Ajmer is one of India's most visited shrines.

qa.q: Amir Khusrau was a disciple of:
qa.e: Khusrau was a devoted disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi.

qa.q: What is a khanqah?
qa.a: A hospice where a Sufi teacher lived with disciples
qa.e: Khanqahs were open to all visitors.

qa.q: What is the langar?
qa.a: A community kitchen where all eat together
qa.e: Started by Guru Nanak, it expresses equality and service.

qa.q: Who compiled the Adi Granth in 1604?
qa.e: Guru Arjan compiled it, including verses of the Gurus and of saints like Kabir and Baba Farid.

qa.q: In which year did Guru Gobind Singh found the Khalsa?
qa.e: The Khalsa was founded at Anandpur Sahib in 1699.

qa.q: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 and passed away in 1539. How many years did he live?
What are miniature paintings?
qa.a: Small, detailed paintings often made for books and albums
qa.e: Their small size and fine detail give them their name.

qa.q: Which artist at Jahangir's court was famous for painting birds and animals?
qa.e: Mansur's nature paintings are known for their accuracy.

qa.q: Who wrote the Akbarnama?
qa.e: Abul Fazl, a courtier of Akbar, wrote this history.

qa.q: The Razmnama is a Persian translation of:
qa.e: Akbar had the Mahabharata translated into Persian as the Razmnama.

qa.q: In which language did Babur write the Baburnama?
qa.e: Babur wrote his memoirs in his mother tongue, a form of Turkish (Chagatai).

qa.q: Who is called the father of Carnatic music?
qa.e: Purandara Dasa composed many songs and basic lessons in Kannada.

qa.q: Krishnadevaraya wrote the Amuktamalyada in:
qa.e: The Vijayanagara king wrote this poem in Telugu.

qa.q: Tansen was a famous musician at the court of:
qa.e: Tansen was one of the 'gems' of Akbar's court.
